result.area_summary: Published practice for governing compiled agent context has converged, remarkably fast (2024-2026), on one dominant form: a Markdown asset with YAML frontmatter, where the frontmatter carries machine-readable loading/trigger metadata (name, description, globs/paths, alwaysApply) and the body carries the instructions, with progressive disclosure via one-level-deep file references. This form recurs across Anthropic Agent Skills (SKILL.md), Cursor rules (.mdc), Claude Code CLAUDE.md/.claude/rules and subagent definitions, Microsoft Prompty (.prompty), and AGENTS.md (frontmatter-less variant). Governance splits into four concerns with distinct established answers: (1) LOADING ECONOMY — progressive disclosure tiers (metadata always in context; body on trigger; references on demand) with published size budgets (SKILL.md under 500 lines, CLAUDE.md under 200 lines, Cursor rules under 500 lines); (2) SCOPE/PRECEDENCE — directory-hierarchy layering (managed/org > user > project > subdirectory, nearest-wins or concatenate-in-order) plus path/glob conditional attachment; (3) VERSIONING — either git-native (files in repo, the dominant practice for rules/skills) or registry-style with version IDs + deployment labels and protected promotion (Langfuse exemplar); (4) TESTING — declarative eval sets of a few scenario cases with expected-behavior rubrics and mixed deterministic/model-graded assertions, built BEFORE writing extensive instructions (Anthropic's evaluation-driven skill development; promptfoo's test-driven config). The survey directly validates the caller's role-prompt-vs-discrete-skill rule: Anthropic's own published guidance draws exactly that line — standing every-session facts belong in CLAUDE.md/role frontmatter+system prompt, while "multi-step procedures that only matter for one activity" must move to skills that load on demand, for both token economy and adherence. Strong adopt candidates: Agent Skills format + authoring checklist, Claude Code memory/rules hierarchy, subagent definition format, promptfoo-style declarative eval sets, and the context-engineering principles (smallest high-signal token set, right-altitude prompts, sectioned structure). Nothing surveyed requires inventing a bespoke format; the residual bespoke need is only in the CONTENT schemas (process-definition outcome/termination fields), not the container form.

findings.name: Anthropic Agent Skills format (SKILL.md) and skill authoring best practices
findings.citation: Anthropic, "Skill authoring best practices," Claude Platform Docs (platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/best-practices); Anthropic Engineering, "Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills" (anthropic.com/engineering/equipping-agents-for-the-real-world-with-agent-skills). Both fetched and verified 2026-08-05.
findings.what_it_defines: A skill is a directory with a SKILL.md (YAML frontmatter + Markdown body) plus optional reference files and executable scripts, loaded via three-tier progressive disclosure: (1) name+description frontmatter pre-loaded into the system prompt at startup, (2) SKILL.md body read only when the skill triggers, (3) bundled files read on demand, scripts executed without loading their contents. The authoring guide prescribes concrete, checkable rules and an evaluation-first development loop.
form_elements: Frontmatter: name (max 64 chars, lowercase/numbers/hyphens, gerund-form naming recommended) and description (max 1,024 chars, non-empty, third person, must state BOTH what the skill does AND when to use it — the description is the sole trigger surface)
SKILL.md body under 500 lines; split into reference files when approaching the limit; references one level deep only; reference files >100 lines get a table of contents
Degrees-of-freedom calibration: high freedom (heuristics) / medium (templates with parameters) / low (exact scripts, 'Do not modify the command') matched to task fragility
Workflow pattern: numbered steps with a copyable progress checklist; feedback-loop pattern: run validator, fix errors, repeat, 'only proceed when validation passes'

Evaluation-driven development: 'Create evaluations BEFORE writing extensive documentation'; eval structure = {skills, query, files, expected_behavior[]} — three scenarios minimum, baseline without the skill, iterate against it
Content rules: no time-sensitive info (use an 'old patterns' section), consistent terminology, concrete examples, provide a default with an escape hatch rather than option lists
Pre-share checklist covering core quality, code/scripts, and testing
findings.fit_notes: Strongest single adopt in the survey. It IS the caller's 'discrete activity in its own skill' rule, published as a standard: one activity per skill, trigger metadata separated from body, token cost paid only on activation (token economy), and per-skill evals (diagnosability — a failing activity maps to one skill file and its three-case eval set). The expected_behavior rubric structure is precisely the requested 'small qualitative fitness-test set' form, and Anthropic notes there is no built-in runner — pairing it with promptfoo (below) closes that gap. The degrees-of-freedom scale is a ready-made vocabulary for the process-definition requirement that definitions carry expected outcomes and termination conditions without becoming a workflow engine.

findings.name: Claude Code CLAUDE.md memory hierarchy and .claude/rules/ path-scoped rules
findings.citation: Anthropic, "How Claude remembers your project," Claude Code Docs (code.claude.com/docs/en/memory). Fetched and verified 2026-08-05.
findings.what_it_defines: The layered persistent-instruction system: CLAUDE.md files at managed-policy, user, project, and local scopes, concatenated root-down (nearest read last); @path imports (max depth four hops); .claude/rules/*.md topic files with optional YAML `paths` frontmatter for glob-conditional loading; subdirectory files loaded on demand when Claude touches those directories; auto-memory with a 200-line/25KB index budget.
form_elements: Scope table: managed policy (cannot be excluded) > user (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) > project (./CLAUDE.md) > local (CLAUDE.local.md, gitignored), loaded broadest-first so specific instructions are read last
Size discipline: 'target under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md file. Longer files consume more context and reduce adherence'

Content discriminator: keep 'facts Claude should hold in every session'; 'If an entry is a multi-step procedure or only matters for one part of the codebase, move it to a skill or a path-scoped rule instead'
Specificity rule: instructions 'concrete enough to verify' ('Use 2-space indentation' not 'Format code properly'); consistency rule: contradictory rules get picked arbitrarily
paths: frontmatter with glob patterns for conditional rule loading; one-topic-per-file rules with descriptive filenames; symlinks for cross-project shared rules
Enforcement boundary: CLAUDE.md is 'context, not enforced configuration' — hard constraints belong in hooks/settings, behavioral guidance in CLAUDE.md
HTML comments stripped before injection (maintainer notes carry zero token cost)
findings.fit_notes: Already the shop's substrate (the repo uses CLAUDE.md @-imports for primers). The valuable governance content is the published discriminators: the standing-facts-vs-procedure line is Anthropic's own statement of the caller's role-prompt/skill split; the context-vs-enforcement line (CLAUDE.md guides, hooks enforce) maps onto the caller's definitions-vs-mechanical-checks derivation rule; the 200-line budget and verifiable-specificity rule are adoptable content-quality guidelines for role primers. The managed-policy layer is a governance pattern for canonical vs shop-local instruction separation the shop already mirrors (.claude/canonical/ vs .claude/shop/).

findings.name: Claude Code subagent definition format (.claude/agents/*.md)
findings.citation: Anthropic, "Create custom subagents," Claude Code Docs (code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents). Fetched and verified 2026-08-05.
findings.what_it_defines: The role-definition file format: Markdown with YAML frontmatter where the body is the subagent's system prompt (its standing identity) and the frontmatter is the delegation and capability contract. Required: name (lowercase-hyphen identifier), description ('When Claude should delegate to this subagent'). Optional: tools/disallowedTools (capability restriction), model, permissionMode, maxTurns, skills (preloaded skill content injected at startup), memory (cross-session learning scope: user/project/local), effort, isolation.
form_elements: Frontmatter/body split: machine-readable routing+capability metadata vs free-text system prompt — identity lives in the body, trigger lives in description
skills: field — the explicit compiled-context join point: named skills' full content injected into the role's context at startup, while unlisted skills remain invokable on demand
tools allowlist as a mechanical constraint derived from role definition (a role that must not implement gets no edit tools)
maxTurns as a termination bound for long-running delegated loops
memory: field giving a role its own persistent cross-session learning store, separate from the main session's
findings.fit_notes: This is the exact container the shop already uses for lead-po/lead-architect and the published form of the caller's rule: role file = standing identity (body) + delegation trigger (description) + capability envelope (tools), with per-activity skills attached via the skills field rather than inlined. Two elements worth deliberately adopting into the seed layer's role-definition schema: the skills preload list as the declared role-to-activity binding (making the compiled context surface enumerable and diffable), and maxTurns as a standard termination field for the process-definition requirement that long-running loops carry termination conditions.

findings.name: AGENTS.md open format
findings.tradition: Cross-vendor open convention (OpenAI Codex, Google Jules, Cursor, Factory, et al.)
findings.citation: agents.md, "AGENTS.md — a simple, open format for guiding coding agents" (https://agents.md/); GitHub repo agentsmd/agents.md. Site fetched and verified 2026-08-05; 60,000+ consuming projects claimed on site.
findings.what_it_defines: 'A dedicated, predictable place to provide the context and instructions to help AI coding agents work on your project': a plain-Markdown file at repo root (no required fields, no frontmatter — 'agents simply parse any headings and text'), complementing README ('READMEs target humans... AGENTS.md contains extra, sometimes detailed context coding agents need'). Nested AGENTS.md files in subdirectories with a nearest-wins precedence rule: 'the closest one takes precedence.' Suggested content: build/test commands, code style, testing instructions, security considerations, 'anything you'd tell a new teammate.'
form_elements: Single well-known filename at a predictable location as the cross-tool contract
Free-form Markdown, deliberately schema-less — governance by convention and location, not validation
Nested-file nearest-wins precedence for monorepos
Human/agent audience split as the organizing principle (vs README)
findings.fit_notes: Context-plus for the shop: Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md, not AGENTS.md (the Claude Code docs prescribe @AGENTS.md import or symlink for interop), and the shop is single-harness, so direct adoption buys nothing today. Its transferable lesson is negative evidence for the seed layer: AGENTS.md's schema-less form is the OPPOSITE of construction-definitions-precede-checks — nothing mechanical can be derived from a file with no required structure. Adopt only the location-as-contract idea (predictable well-known paths per definition type); reject the schema-less content model for anything checks must be derived from.

findings.name: Cursor project rules (.cursor/rules/*.mdc)
findings.citation: Cursor, "Rules," official docs (cursor.com/docs/context/rules). Fetched and verified 2026-08-05.
findings.what_it_defines: 'Rules provide persistent, reusable context at the prompt level.' Each rule is an .mdc file (Markdown + YAML frontmatter) in .cursor/rules/, with frontmatter fields description, globs, alwaysApply. Which fields are set determines one of four activation modes: Always Apply (every session), Apply Intelligently (agent evaluates description for relevance), Apply to Specific Files (glob match), Apply Manually (@-mention). Nested .cursor/rules/ directories scope rules to subtrees; Team Rules (enterprise) take precedence and are enforced from a dashboard.
form_elements: Four-mode activation taxonomy encoded entirely in frontmatter field combinations — loading policy as declarative metadata, not prose
'Keep rules under 500 lines' and 'Split large rules into multiple, composable rules'
'Provide concrete examples or referenced files' — reference canonical code rather than duplicating it, so rules stay current
Org-level Team Rules with precedence over project rules (centralized governance layer)
findings.fit_notes: The distinctive contribution is the explicit four-mode activation taxonomy: it names the loading-policy dimension (always / model-judged / path-conditional / manual) that Claude Code spreads across CLAUDE.md, paths: rules, and skills. Adapt the taxonomy as vocabulary in the seed layer's definition-of-a-definition: every compiled-context artifact should declare which activation mode it uses and why — directly serving token economy (nothing always-on that could be conditional) and diagnosability (a misfire is classified as wrong-mode vs wrong-content). The .mdc container itself is redundant with the Claude-native forms the shop already runs.

findings.name: llms.txt
findings.citation: Jeremy Howard, "/llms.txt — a proposal to provide information to help LLMs use websites," Answer.AI, Sept 3, 2024 (answer.ai/posts/2024-09-03-llmstxt.html); specification at llmstxt.org. Spec fetched and verified 2026-08-05.
findings.what_it_defines: A standardized /llms.txt file giving LLMs a curated, context-window-sized entry point to a site: required H1 (project name), blockquote summary, optional prose sections, then H2-delimited 'file lists' — markdown link lists where each entry is '[name](url)' optionally followed by ': notes'. An 'Optional' H2 section marks content omissible under context pressure. Companion convention: serve .md versions of pages at URL+'.md'. Adopted in the wild as an index/full-text pair (llms.txt navigation + llms-full.txt concatenation); tooling (llms_txt2ctx) expands the index into an XML context file.
form_elements: Fixed minimal grammar: H1 → blockquote summary → sections → H2 link-lists with per-link annotations
Curation-over-crawling: a human-selected, annotated map of what matters, sized for a context window
Explicit 'Optional' tier — degradation order declared in the artifact itself
Parallel .md rendering of canonical content for machine consumption
findings.fit_notes: Not a rules format but the cleanest published INDEX form for progressive disclosure: name + one-line summary + annotated links + an explicit optional tier. Adapt it as the shape of the shop's catalog surfaces — a skills/definitions index the router or a role loads first (the shop's lazy 'shop-templates show' load-on-entry already needs exactly such a manifest), and note Anthropic's own docs now emit llms.txt (observed on code.claude.com and modelcontextprotocol.io during this survey). The 'Optional' tier is a published precedent for declaring token-economy degradation order inside a definition artifact. Ecosystem caveat: crawler adoption for the SEO use is disputed; that criticism does not touch the inference-time index use relevant here.

findings.name: MCP server prompts primitive
findings.tradition: Protocol standard (Model Context Protocol, Anthropic-originated open spec)
findings.citation: Model Context Protocol Specification 2025-06-18, "Prompts" (modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/prompts). Fetched and verified 2026-08-05.
findings.what_it_defines: Prompts as 'user-controlled' reusable templates a server exposes for explicit selection (e.g., slash commands): each has name (unique id), optional title, description, and typed arguments list; clients discover via prompts/list, instantiate via prompts/get with argument substitution; servers SHOULD emit notifications/prompts/list_changed when the prompt set changes. Prompt messages may embed server-managed resources directly.
form_elements: Named, argument-typed template contract (name/title/description/arguments[]) — the prompt's interface separated from its body
Explicit control-plane taxonomy: prompts are user-controlled, distinct from application-controlled resources and model-controlled tools
list_changed notification — a protocol-level change-propagation hook for the prompt inventory
Embedded resources for composing server-managed reference content into a template
findings.fit_notes: Context-only for the seed layer: the shop's compiled context is file-based, not protocol-served, and MCP's prompt body carries no authoring or quality prescriptions. Its lasting contribution is the three-way control taxonomy (user-controlled / application-controlled / model-controlled), useful vocabulary when the seed layer classifies who may cause a given definition to enter context — e.g., the shop's skills are model-controlled (description-triggered) while slash-invoked skills are user-controlled. Revisit as adopt only if shop-templates ever serves role/skill definitions to BC containers over a protocol rather than files.

findings.name: MCP server resources primitive and annotations
findings.citation: Model Context Protocol Specification 2025-06-18, "Resources" (modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/resources). Fetched and verified 2026-08-05.
findings.what_it_defines: Resources as 'application-driven' read-only context, each uniquely identified by an RFC 3986 URI, with metadata (name, title, description, mimeType, size), parameterized resource templates (RFC 6570 URI templates), list/read/subscribe operations, and optional annotations: audience (['user'|'assistant']), priority (0.0-1.0, 'A value of 1 means most important (effectively required), while 0 means least important (entirely optional)'), and lastModified (ISO 8601).
form_elements: Stable URI identity for every context artifact
Annotation vocabulary: audience / priority / lastModified as standardized inclusion-decision metadata
Subscription + list_changed as change-notification for context artifacts
Application-driven inclusion: the host, not the model, decides what enters context
findings.fit_notes: The annotations block is the adaptable piece: audience/priority/lastModified is a small published vocabulary for exactly the metadata the seed layer's artifact-schema definitions need so that inclusion decisions and staleness checks can be mechanically derived rather than judged per-use (Claude Code's auto-memory 'modified' frontmatter field, verified above, is the same idea independently converging). Adapt the field vocabulary into the frontmatter schema of shop definition artifacts; the protocol machinery itself is not needed on a file-based lead host.

findings.name: Registry-style prompt version control (Langfuse exemplar)
findings.tradition: LLMOps / prompt management platforms (Langfuse; same pattern in LangSmith, PromptLayer)
findings.citation: Langfuse, "Prompt Version Control" and "Prompt Management overview," official docs (langfuse.com/docs/prompt-management/features/prompt-version-control). Fetched and verified 2026-08-05.
findings.what_it_defines: Prompts managed as registry objects rather than hardcoded strings: every change mints an automatic version ID; mutable labels point at versions ('Labels can be used to assign prompts to environments (staging, production), tenants..., or experiments'); a 'production' label is the served default and 'latest' auto-tracks; rollback is retargeting the label ('set the production label to that previous version'); diffs between versions; protected labels restrict promotion to admin/owner roles; client-side caching makes retrieval deployment-decoupled and zero-latency.
form_elements: Immutable version + mutable deployment label as the core versioning algebra
Protected labels — promotion to production as a permissioned act, separate from authoring
Version diffs as the review surface for prompt change
Prompt deployment decoupled from application deployment
findings.fit_notes: Describes the registry school; the shop's prompts-in-git school (all rules/skills surveys above) already gets immutable versions, diffs, and review from git itself, so adopting a registry product is unjustified. What transfers is the algebra: (a) protected promotion — a definition change becoming 'what compiled agents actually run' should be a distinct, gated act (in git terms: canonical templates updated only via the shopsystem-templates BC pipeline, which the shop already enforces by convention — this names and justifies it); (b) the deployed-version pointer — each shop/BC should record WHICH version of each canonical definition it is running, so behavior regressions are diagnosable to a definition version. Recommending the pattern, not the platform.

findings.name: promptfoo declarative eval configuration
findings.citation: promptfoo, "Introduction," official docs (promptfoo.dev/docs/intro/). Fetched and verified 2026-08-05.
findings.what_it_defines: 'Test-driven prompt engineering is much more effective than trial-and-error': a declarative YAML config declaring prompts, providers, and test cases with per-case assertions mixing deterministic checks (contains, regex, JSON validity) and model-graded rubrics; evals run locally and in CI as regression gates; the same harness extends to red-teaming. Explicitly positioned as unit testing for prompts — small named cases, automated scoring, diffable matrix output across prompt versions.
form_elements: Config triple: prompts × providers × tests, versioned as code alongside the prompts
Assertion taxonomy: deterministic metrics AND model-graded (rubric) assertions in the same case — mechanical checks and qualitative judgment sharing one file format
CI integration: prompt-change PRs gated on eval regressions
Small named scenario cases rather than large statistical benchmarks
findings.fit_notes: Directly fills the caller's 'small qualitative fitness-test sets for non-deterministic output' slot with an established, git-native form, and closes the gap Anthropic's skill-eval guidance leaves open (Anthropic defines the eval structure but ships no runner). Fit with the derivation principle is exact: the skill/role definition is the construction standard; a per-skill promptfooconfig (or an equivalent minimal YAML in the shop's own harness) holds 3-10 cases whose rubric assertions are derived from that definition's expected_behavior lines. Adopt the FORM (declarative cases + mixed assertion taxonomy, colocated with the definition, run on definition change); tool choice itself can be swapped without losing the form.

findings.name: Microsoft Prompty (.prompty asset format)
findings.tradition: Prompt-as-code asset formats (Microsoft; related: Google Genkit dotprompt)
findings.citation: Prompty, "The .prompty File Format," prompty.ai/core-concepts/file-format; specification (Prompty.yaml) in the microsoft/prompty GitHub repository. Verified via prompty.ai documentation and the microsoft/prompty repo, 2026-08-05.
findings.what_it_defines: A language-agnostic single-file prompt asset: YAML frontmatter declaring metadata, model configuration, declared inputs and outputs, and optional sample data for testing, above a Jinja-templated Markdown body that becomes the prompt instructions. Positioned as an 'asset class' for observability, understandability, and portability, with a published machine-readable spec (Prompty.yaml) and runtimes across languages.
form_elements: Declared inputs/outputs in frontmatter — the prompt's I/O contract made machine-checkable, separate from its prose
Embedded sample data — a smoke test shipped inside the asset itself
Formal spec file (Prompty.yaml) validating the asset format — the format itself is schema-governed
Template body with explicit variable binding rather than ad-hoc string interpolation
findings.fit_notes: The shop won't use .prompty files (Claude-native containers win locally), but Prompty contributes the one element the Anthropic formats lack: an explicit, validatable I/O contract plus embedded sample data in the asset's frontmatter. Adapt into the seed layer's process/skill definition schema as required frontmatter fields — expected inputs, expected outputs/outcomes, and at least one worked sample — which is precisely the caller's requirement that process definitions carry expected outcomes and outputs, and it makes the mechanical-check derivation (validate frontmatter against Prompty-style schema) nearly free. Also the strongest published precedent that a definition format should itself be schema-validated.

findings.name: Anthropic context-engineering principles (right altitude, minimal high-signal token set)
findings.citation: Anthropic Engineering, "Effective context engineering for AI agents" (anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents). Fetched and verified 2026-08-05.
findings.what_it_defines: The principle layer under all the formats above: context is a finite resource subject to 'context rot,' so the goal is 'the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of some desired outcome.' System prompts should sit at the 'right altitude' — 'specific enough to guide behavior effectively, yet flexible enough to provide the model with strong heuristics' — and be organized 'into distinct sections (like <background_information>, <instructions>, ## Tool guidance, ## Output description...)' via XML tags or Markdown headers. Prescribes just-in-time retrieval (lightweight identifiers loaded on demand), compaction, structured note-taking (external memory files), and sub-agent architectures returning condensed 1,000-2,000-token summaries.
form_elements: Right-altitude criterion for role/system prompts — the published test between brittle hardcoded logic and vague guidance
Sectioned prompt organization with named canonical sections
Minimal-high-signal-token objective as the token-economy first principle
JIT retrieval via lightweight identifiers — the theoretical basis for skills/rules progressive disclosure
Sub-agents as context isolation with condensed-summary return contracts
findings.fit_notes: Adopt as the seed layer's principle statements rather than as a format: these are citable first principles from which the shop's format choices (skills over inline procedure, role primers under a line budget, subagent summary contracts) DERIVE — matching the caller's construction-definitions-precede-checks architecture at the principle level. The named-sections prescription is an adoptable content-quality guideline for role prompts; the right-altitude criterion belongs in the review rubric derived for any role-definition change; the condensed-summary return contract is a ready form for the process-definition requirement that long-running/delegated loops define their terminating output.

result.area_summary: Qualitative evaluation of non-deterministic LLM output has a well-established, convergent shape across research and production tooling: (1) a small, task-specific set of test cases (input/context per case), (2) plain-language grading criteria or rubrics attached to each case or dimension, and (3) an LLM judge that grades output against those criteria, returning pass/fail or a scale plus a reason — calibrated against human judgment and hardened against known judge biases. The research base is solid: Zheng et al. (NeurIPS 2023) established LLM-as-judge viability and named its failure modes (position, verbosity, self-enhancement bias); the ICLR 2025 "null models" paper proved judges are adversarially gameable; Shankar et al. (UIST 2024) showed evaluation criteria cannot be fully defined a priori ("criteria drift") and must be calibrated iteratively against human grades; G-Eval (EMNLP 2023) gave the canonical criteria→evaluation-steps→score judging procedure. Production frameworks (promptfoo, DeepEval, Ragas, OpenEvals/LangSmith, Braintrust autoevals, OpenAI evals) all implement this same rubric-judged pattern, mostly as declarative config — promptfoo's scenarios+llm-rubric YAML and LangWatch's Scenario judge-agent framework are the closest living relatives of scenario-shaped, criteria-judged testing. Directly Gherkin-syntaxed fitness tests judged (not executed) by an LLM has no established standard implementation — the BDD×LLM literature runs the other direction (LLMs generating/assessing Gherkin) — so the product authority's proposal is a syntax adaptation of an established pattern, not an established form itself. Verdict on the proposal: ADAPT — the underlying pattern (scenario + natural-language expected properties + LLM judge, small set per output type) is orthodox practice; the Gherkin surface syntax is a justified bespoke twist given the shop's existing Gherkin literacy, provided Then-clauses are held to falsifiability discipline, judged features are segregated from executable features, and judges are bias-hardened and human-calibrated.

findings.name: LLM-as-a-judge foundational research (MT-Bench, Zheng et al. 2023)
findings.citation: Zheng, L. et al., "Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena," NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (arXiv:2306.05685)
findings.what_it_defines: Establishes that strong LLMs grading open-ended output can reach high agreement with human preference (~80%+ with GPT-4 on MT-Bench), and names the canonical judge failure modes: position bias (favoring an answer by placement), verbosity bias (favoring longer answers), self-enhancement bias (favoring the judge's own model family), and limited reasoning ability on math/logic. Proposes mitigations: swapping positions, few-shot judging, reference-guided grading, chain-of-thought.
form_elements: Pairwise comparison vs. single-answer grading as two judge modes
Position-swap to detect/cancel position bias
Reference-guided judging (give the judge a reference answer)
Chain-of-thought before verdict
Agreement-with-human measurement as the meta-metric for judge quality
findings.fit_notes: This is the evidence base any LLM-judged fitness-test layer must be designed against, not a format to adopt. For the shop's seed layer it dictates derived-check design rules: use single-output grading against explicit criteria (not pairwise, which imports position bias), prefer a different model family for judging than generating (self-preference), instruct the judge that length/effort is not merit (verbosity), and require reasoning-before-verdict. These rules belong in the judge-role definition that gets compiled into the reviewing agent's context.

findings.name: Judge gameability: null-model benchmark cheating (ICLR 2025)
findings.citation: Zheng, X. et al., "Cheating Automatic LLM Benchmarks: Null Models Achieve High Win Rates," ICLR 2025 Oral (arXiv:2410.07137)
findings.what_it_defines: Demonstrates that a null model emitting a constant, input-irrelevant adversarial response achieves top-ranked win rates on judge-scored benchmarks (86.5% LC win rate on AlpacaEval 2.0, 83.0 on Arena-Hard-Auto, 9.55 on MT-Bench), proving LLM judges are structurally gameable by output that manipulates the grading prompt rather than doing the task. Calls for anti-cheating mechanisms in automatic evaluation.
form_elements: Adversarial constant-output attack on judge prompts
Transferability of cheating outputs across unseen test instructions
Anti-cheating requirement as a design constraint for judge pipelines
findings.fit_notes: Directly relevant threat model for the shop: the generating agent and the judging agent are both LLMs inside one system, so Goodharting is a live risk — a generator optimized (even implicitly, via retry loops) against a known rubric can learn to satisfy the judge without satisfying the intent. Mitigations for the derived-check layer: keep judge prompts/rubrics out of the generator's context where feasible, delimit and label the evaluated artifact as untrusted data in the judge prompt, spot-audit judge verdicts with human review, and never treat judge pass-rate as the sole gate for high-stakes artifacts.

findings.name: G-Eval criteria-to-steps judging procedure
findings.citation: Liu, Y. et al., "G-Eval: NLG Evaluation using GPT-4 with Better Human Alignment," EMNLP 2023, pp. 2511–2522 (arXiv:2303.16634); productionized as DeepEval's GEval metric
findings.what_it_defines: The canonical procedure for turning a short natural-language quality criterion into a reproducible LLM grading run: (1) the judge LLM auto-expands the criterion into explicit chain-of-thought evaluation steps, (2) grades via a form-filling paradigm against those steps, (3) optionally weights the score by output-token probabilities for finer granularity. Achieved the then-best human correlation on summarization quality (Spearman 0.514).
form_elements: criteria: one-paragraph plain-language quality definition
evaluation_steps: enumerated checks derived from the criteria (auto-generated or hand-fixed)
evaluation_params: which artifact fields the judge sees (input, output, context, reference)
1–N scale score with threshold, plus judge reason
findings.fit_notes: Strong structural fit with the shop's founding principle that checks are DERIVED from construction definitions: G-Eval is literally a derivation procedure (definition → evaluation steps → grade). For the seed layer, the criteria + fixed evaluation_steps pair is an adoptable micro-format for each fitness test regardless of execution framework; hand-pinning the evaluation steps (rather than letting the judge re-derive them per run) trades a little alignment for determinism and auditability, which suits a quality layer that must be reviewable.

findings.name: EvalGen / criteria drift (Who Validates the Validators)
findings.citation: Shankar, S. et al., "Who Validates the Validators? Aligning LLM-Assisted Evaluation of LLM Outputs with Human Preferences," UIST 2024 (arXiv:2404.12272)
findings.what_it_defines: A mixed-initiative workflow (EvalGen) for authoring evaluation criteria and their implementations (code assertions or LLM-judge prompts), selecting implementations by alignment with human grades on sampled outputs. Its central empirical finding is criteria drift: humans need to grade outputs to discover their criteria, so evaluation criteria cannot be fully specified a priori and are partially dependent on the outputs observed.
form_elements: Criteria list authored per task, each implemented as code assertion or judge prompt
Human grading of sampled outputs as alignment signal
Implementation selection by agreement with human grades
Iterative criteria revision as outputs are observed
findings.fit_notes: Two direct consequences for the shop's seed layer. First, the fitness-test sets must be versioned living artifacts with an explicit revision loop fed by human (product-authority) spot-grading — a static fire-and-forget test set contradicts the criteria-drift evidence. Second, it legitimizes the 'small set' framing in the proposal: EvalGen-style practice starts from a handful of criteria and grows them from observed failures, not from exhaustive upfront enumeration. The full EvalGen tooling is not needed; the calibration loop is the adaptable practice.

findings.name: promptfoo declarative rubric assertions and scenarios
findings.citation: promptfoo documentation: model-graded metrics, llm-rubric assertion, and scenarios config (promptfoo/promptfoo on GitHub)
findings.what_it_defines: A declarative YAML eval format: test cases carry vars (inputs/context) and assert blocks; the llm-rubric assertion type states a plain-language expected property ('is concise and apologetic', 'does not invent facts') that a grader model scores, returning pass/score/reason. The scenarios construct groups shared data (config: vars sets) with a set of tests run against each — a matrix of context × expectations. Also ships g-eval, factuality, select-best, and classifier assertions.
form_elements: tests[].vars — the Given/When analog (input and context)
tests[].assert[] with type: llm-rubric and value: <natural-language criterion> — the Then analog
scenarios[] — config (vars sets) crossed with tests
Grader provider pinning and per-assertion thresholds
Assertions co-resident with deterministic checks (regex, json, contains) in one file
findings.fit_notes: The closest established, adoptable FORMAT to what the shop needs: it already is 'scenario + natural-language fitness assertions judged by an LLM, alongside mechanical checks' in a stable, documented, widely-used YAML form. The vars/assert structure is semantically isomorphic to Given-When/Then. Adopting promptfoo's format (or its schema as the interchange shape) would satisfy the strong-preference-for-established-forms rule; the shop's Gherkin surface could compile down to it. Caveat: the format is tool-coupled and per-test-case, not artifact-type-schema-aware — it would sit at the derived-check layer, not the definition layer.

findings.name: DeepEval G-Eval metric implementation
findings.citation: DeepEval documentation, "G-Eval" metric (Confident AI / deepeval)
findings.what_it_defines: Pytest-style Python eval framework whose GEval metric implements the G-Eval paper for arbitrary custom criteria: define criteria or explicit evaluation_steps, select evaluation_params (input/actual output/expected output/context), get a probability-weighted 0–1 score with threshold and reason. Positioned as the framework's most versatile metric for any custom qualitative dimension.
form_elements: LLMTestCase: input, actual_output, expected_output, retrieval_context
GEval(criteria=... | evaluation_steps=[...], threshold=...)
Score + reason output per test case
CI integration via pytest-style assertions
findings.fit_notes: Confirms the criteria/evaluation_steps pair as a de facto industry micro-format (same shape as the paper). Less attractive than promptfoo as a FORMAT for the shop because the definition lives in Python code rather than declarative artifact files — the shop's seed layer wants tool-independent definitional documents. Useful as an execution backend or as schema inspiration for the fitness-test document type.

findings.name: Ragas rubric-based scoring and AspectCritique
findings.tradition: Production LLM eval tooling (open source, RAG-origin)
findings.citation: Ragas documentation: Rubric-Based Evaluation and Aspect Critique metrics
findings.what_it_defines: Two reusable judged-metric shapes: (a) rubric-based scoring — a score-anchored rubric with a written description per score level (1–5), used for domain-specific quality; (b) AspectCritique — binary yes/no judgment against a single named aspect (harmfulness, conciseness, or user-defined criteria). Plus the RAG-specific judged metrics (faithfulness, answer relevance, context precision/recall) it popularized.
form_elements: Score-anchored rubric: explicit description for each score level
Binary aspect critique: one aspect, one yes/no criterion
Component-wise metric decomposition (faithfulness vs relevance vs context quality)
findings.fit_notes: The score-anchored rubric (a written description per level, not just a bare 1–5 scale) is the established form the shop should use anywhere a graded rather than binary verdict is wanted — bare Likert scales without level descriptions are known to judge inconsistently. The binary aspect-critique shape maps naturally onto a single Then-clause. Ragas as a tool is RAG-centric and not otherwise a fit.

findings.name: LangSmith / OpenEvals judge evaluators
findings.citation: LangChain, openevals library and LangSmith evaluation docs ("Evaluating Large Language Models With OpenEvals"; LangSmith evaluation concepts)
findings.what_it_defines: Prebuilt and factory-built LLM-as-judge evaluators (correctness, conciseness, helpfulness, plus custom rubric prompts) run against datasets of examples or live traces; documented authoring guidance: state exactly what constitutes good/bad, choose binary over continuous where possible, include few-shot examples of good and bad outputs, allow custom output schemas.
form_elements: Dataset of examples (input, optional reference output)
Judge prompt template with rubric and few-shot good/bad exemplars
Binary-preferred scoring guidance
Offline (dataset) vs online (trace) evaluation split
findings.fit_notes: Its authoring guidance (binary-preferred verdicts, exemplar-anchored rubrics) matches the rest of the field and should inform the shop's content-quality-guideline format. As tooling it is platform-coupled (LangSmith) and adds no format element promptfoo/DeepEval don't already provide; survey-level context rather than an adoption candidate.

findings.name: Braintrust autoevals scorer library
findings.tradition: Production LLM eval tooling (commercial + OSS library)
findings.citation: Braintrust, autoevals library (braintrustdata/autoevals on GitHub) and "LLM-as-a-judge scorers and classifiers" docs
findings.what_it_defines: Open-source library of preconfigured LLM-judge scorers (Factuality, ClosedQA, Summarization, etc.) and the LLMClassifierFromTemplate pattern: a judge prompt plus an explicit choice→score mapping (e.g., A=1.0, B=0.5, C=0.0), which forces the judge into a constrained classification rather than freeform scoring; scores normalized 0–100%.
form_elements: Choice-based classification with explicit choice_scores mapping
Prompt-template scorer definition (portable, YAML-representable)
Code scorers and judge scorers under one scorer interface
findings.fit_notes: The choice→score mapping (constrained enumeration of verdict options with defined meanings) is a judge-reliability technique worth folding into the shop's judge-prompt conventions — it reduces scoring variance versus asking for a free 1–10. Otherwise ecosystem-redundant with promptfoo/DeepEval for the shop's purposes.

findings.name: OpenAI evals framework and eval design guidance
findings.citation: OpenAI, evals framework (openai/evals on GitHub: build-eval.md, model-graded eval templates in JSON/YAML registry) and "Evaluation best practices" developer guide
findings.what_it_defines: The original open registry format for evals: JSONL datasets plus YAML eval definitions; model-graded templates (fact, closedqa, battle) where a judge model compares output to ideal answers or grades against a criterion — the direct ancestor of promptfoo's model-graded assertions. The developer-platform guidance covers designing graders and eval-driven development. Note: the hosted Evals platform is being deprecated (read-only Oct 2026, shutdown Nov 2026); the open-source repo and the guidance remain the citable prior art.
form_elements: JSONL sample format (input, ideal)
YAML eval registry entry (eval class + args + dataset ref)
Model-graded template: prompt with {output} and {criteria}/{ideal} slots, constrained verdict choices
Two-stage answer-then-judge flow
findings.fit_notes: Historically important as the form most later tools copied; the model-graded template with constrained verdict choices is the same micro-format as Braintrust's classifier and promptfoo's rubric. Given the hosted platform's deprecation and the repo's benchmark-registry orientation, it is prior-art context and format precedent rather than an adoption target.

findings.name: Anthropic eval-writing guidance
findings.citation: Anthropic, "Define success criteria and build evaluations" (Claude platform docs) and "Demystifying evals for AI agents" (Anthropic engineering blog)
findings.what_it_defines: Provider-canonical practice for eval authoring: SMART-style success criteria; design principles (task-specific with edge cases; automate when possible; prefer volume of lower-signal automated grading over few hand-graded items); a grader hierarchy — deterministic/code-based where possible, LLM graders where necessary, humans judiciously for calibration; LLM-grading mechanics (different model for judging than generating, one isolated judge per quality dimension, constrained output like 'output only the number', defined scale anchors, allow 'Unknown', frequent calibration against expert human judgment).
form_elements: Success-criteria statement format (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant)
Grader hierarchy: code-based → LLM-based → human
One-dimension-per-judge isolation rule
Likert/binary/ordinal grading prompt patterns with anchored scales
Calibration loop against human judgment
findings.fit_notes: Directly adoptable as the authoring standard for the shop's fitness-test sets and the judge conventions derived from them: the grader hierarchy operationalizes 'mechanical checks first, LLM rubric only for what code cannot check', which matches the shop's definitions-precede-checks principle, and the one-dimension-per-judge rule dictates that a multi-clause fitness set be judged clause-by-clause, not holistically. This is guidance to encode into role/skill definitions, not a file format.

findings.name: CheckList behavioral testing methodology
findings.citation: Ribeiro, M.T., Wu, T., Guestrin, C., Singh, S., "Beyond Accuracy: Behavioral Testing of NLP Models with CheckList," ACL 2020 Best Paper (arXiv:2005.04118)
findings.what_it_defines: A task-agnostic behavioral-testing methodology for NLP systems borrowed from software behavioral testing: a matrix of linguistic capabilities × three test types — Minimum Functionality Tests (small targeted unit-like probes), Invariance tests (perturbations that must not change output), and Directional expectation tests (perturbations that must change output a known way). Empirically, practitioners with CheckList wrote 2x the tests and found ~3x the bugs.
form_elements: Capability × test-type matrix for test ideation
MFT: minimal targeted probe with expected behavior
INV: perturbation + output-invariance expectation
DIR: perturbation + expected direction of change
Template-based case generation for coverage
findings.fit_notes: The strongest pre-LLM precedent for the proposal's 'small set of targeted qualitative tests' framing: MFTs are exactly small behavioral probes rather than exhaustive suites, and the capability×test-type matrix is a disciplined ideation device the shop can reuse when deriving fitness sets from construction definitions. INV/DIR test types translate to LLM-judged form (e.g., 'restating the brief in different words must not change the verdict'). Methodology to adapt; the tooling itself targets classifier-era NLP.

findings.name: Giskard agent testing and scan
findings.citation: Giskard-AI/giskard-oss (GitHub) and Giskard documentation: LLM scan, test suites, agent evaluation
findings.what_it_defines: An evaluation/testing library for ML models and LLM agents: automated scan generating adversarial test suites from a plain-language agent description (prompt injection, harmful content, hallucination, robustness classes), plus persistent domain test suites for regression testing agent behavior across versions, combining heuristic and LLM-assisted detectors.
form_elements: Plain-language agent description as scan seed
Vulnerability-class taxonomy (hallucination, injection, bias, robustness, disclosure)
Persistent test suite object re-run across model/agent versions
Heuristic + LLM-judge detector pairing
findings.fit_notes: Despite occasionally being described alongside BDD, Giskard is not a Given-When-Then framework — its relevance is the pattern of deriving a test suite from a natural-language behavior description (cousin to the shop's derive-checks-from-definitions principle) and its vulnerability-class taxonomy, useful when the fitness sets must cover robustness/safety dimensions, not just content quality. Context and taxonomy source, not a format to adopt.

findings.name: LangWatch Scenario: simulation-based agent testing with judge agent
findings.citation: langwatch/scenario (GitHub) — "Agentic testing for agentic codebases"; LangWatch agent-simulation docs
findings.what_it_defines: An agent-testing framework where each test is a named scenario: a described situation, a simulated user driving a multi-turn interaction, and a Judge Agent holding a list of plain-language criteria that it evaluates at every turn, deciding pass/fail/continue. Scenarios run in CI. This is the closest living implementation of 'scenario-shaped test whose assertions are natural-language criteria evaluated by an LLM rather than executed as code'.
form_elements: Scenario: name + situation description (Given/When analog)
criteria: [list of natural-language expectations] (Then analog)
JudgeAgent evaluating criteria per turn with verdict + reasoning
UserSimulatorAgent for multi-turn drive
CI-runnable script per scenario
findings.fit_notes: Direct prior art for the product authority's proposal minus the Gherkin keywords: it demonstrates the pattern is viable and shipping in an established OSS tool, and its structure (situation + criteria list + judge) is exactly what a judged Gherkin scenario compiles to. For the shop, its multi-turn user simulation is more machinery than the artifact-fitness use case needs, but its scenario/criteria/judge schema is the strongest external validation that the proposed form works. Adapt: borrow the schema semantics, keep the shop's Gherkin surface syntax.

findings.name: BDD-for-AI prior art: LLMs and Gherkin intersect in the other direction
findings.citation: Representative primary sources: "Comprehensive Evaluation and Insights into the Use of LLMs in the Automation of BDD Acceptance Test Formulation" (arXiv:2403.14965); "From Law to Gherkin" (arXiv:2508.20744); "Epic-Organized vs. Requirement-Aligned Gherkin: An Empirical Evaluation of LLM-Based Acceptance Criteria Generation" (SEET 2026, arXiv:2607.01980); LLM-as-a-Judge rubric evaluation of Gherkin artifacts (arXiv:2512.01232)
findings.what_it_defines: The published BDD×LLM literature covers: LLMs generating Gherkin scenarios from requirements/regulations; empirical quality evaluation of that generated Gherkin (including rubric-driven LLM-as-judge assessment of scenario completeness, criteria alignment, and assertion quality); and classic executable BDD (Cucumber/behave step definitions). What it does NOT contain is an established, named standard for the inverse pattern — authoring G/W/T scenarios as fitness specifications for LLM output and having an LLM judge (rather than step-definition code) evaluate the Then-clauses. That exact pattern exists only as near-neighbors (LangWatch Scenario's criteria lists, promptfoo's rubric assertions) and scattered experiments.
form_elements: Gherkin G/W/T as LLM-parseable and LLM-generatable structure (empirically supported)
Rubric dimensions used when LLMs judge Gherkin quality: completeness, criteria alignment, assertion specificity
Executable-BDD convention: every step binds to a step definition (the cultural default the proposal breaks)
findings.fit_notes: Establishes two things for the proposal assessment: (1) Gherkin's structured natural language is demonstrably friendly to LLM consumption, supporting the reuse-one-literacy argument; (2) there is no external standard to simply adopt for judge-evaluated Gherkin, so that specific combination is bespoke and needs the justification the shop's rules demand — the justification available is that it is a thin syntax layer over the well-established scenario+criteria+judge pattern. Also flags the cultural risk: in every established Gherkin ecosystem, scenarios are assumed executable, so judged-not-executed features need unmistakable marking.

findings.name: Gherkin-as-qualitative-fitness proposal
findings.tradition: Internal proposal (shopsystem product authority), assessed against external evidence
findings.citation: Product authority proposal (verbatim, internal): "Use Given/When/Then Gherkin/BDD form tests to establish fitness... as long as it is understood they won't be backed by typical code-style implementation... at least a small set of tests to evaluate fitness of any given generated output." Assessed against: LangWatch Scenario (github.com/langwatch/scenario), promptfoo llm-rubric/scenarios (promptfoo.dev), G-Eval (arXiv:2303.16634), Zheng et al. (arXiv:2306.05685), null-model cheating (arXiv:2410.07137), EvalGen criteria drift (arXiv:2404.12272), Anthropic eval guidance (anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents), CheckList (arXiv:2005.04118)
findings.what_it_defines: Proposal: express qualitative fitness tests for non-deterministic LLM-generated output as Given/When/Then Gherkin scenarios, explicitly NOT backed by executable step definitions — evaluated instead by an LLM reviewer — with a small (not extensive) set per generated-output type.
form_elements: Feature file per artifact/output type, tagged non-executable (e.g., @judged / kept outside executable features/ tree)
Given = artifact context and inputs available to the judge; When = the generation activity under test; Then/And = one falsifiable, observable quality property per clause
Per-clause binary verdict + judge reasoning (one dimension per judgment, per Anthropic guidance)
Compilation target: each Then-clause maps 1:1 to a rubric assertion (promptfoo llm-rubric / criteria-list entry / G-Eval evaluation step)
Calibration record: periodic human (product-authority) grading of sampled verdicts per EvalGen criteria-drift finding
findings.fit_notes: VERDICT: ADAPT — sound pattern, bespoke surface syntax, adoptable with guardrails. PRIOR ART: the exact combination (Gherkin syntax + LLM judge instead of step definitions) has no established named standard — BDD×LLM literature runs the other direction (LLMs generating/assessing Gherkin). But the underlying semantics are firmly established: LangWatch Scenario ships scenario-shaped tests whose assertions are plain-language criteria evaluated by a Judge Agent; promptfoo's scenarios+llm-rubric YAML is structurally isomorphic (vars=Given/When, rubric assertion=Then); G-Eval canonizes criteria→steps→judged-score. So the proposal is a thin syntax adaptation of orthodox practice, which satisfies the shop's bespoke-requires-justification bar: the justification is literacy reuse — Gherkin is already this shop's behavior-contract vocabulary (features/ tree, scenario hashes, assign_scenarios), so PO-authored fitness tests need no second formalism, and the research above confirms G/W/T is LLM-friendly structure. STRENGTHS: (1) single authoring literacy across behavior contracts and fitness tests; (2) G/W/T forces context (Given) and activity (When) to be explicit, which judge prompts need anyway; (3) one-clause-one-property structure aligns with Anthropic's isolated-dimension judging rule; (4) 'small set' matches CheckList MFT practice and EvalGen's grow-from-observed-failures finding — small is the established norm for qualitative sets, not a compromise. FAILURE MODES: (1) unfalsifiable Then-clauses ('Then the brief is compelling') — the judge will happily pass vibes; mitigation: authoring rule that every Then names an observable property whose violation a reviewer could point at, plus score-anchored or binary phrasing (Ragas rubric form, Braintrust choice_scores); (2) judge gameability/Goodharting (null-model result, self-preference, verbosity bias) — mitigation: judge model/context separated from generator, artifact delimited as untrusted data, reasoning-before-verdict, spot-audits by human; (3) executable-culture confusion — every established Gherkin ecosystem assumes step definitions exist, so judged features WILL eventually be fed to a runner or 'fixed' by an agent that binds steps; mitigation: hard segregation (distinct directory such as fitness/ not features/, mandatory tag, header comment stating evaluation semantics) and a schema-level marker in the artifact-type definition; (4) criteria drift — mitigation: fitness sets are versioned artifacts with a standing calibration loop (sampled human grading), not immutable specs; (5) silent judge variance — mitigation: pin judge model and prompt template version alongside the feature file. ALTERNATIVES DOING THE SAME JOB: adopt promptfoo YAML directly (established format, loses Gherkin literacy, gains executability of the eval harness); LangWatch Scenario criteria lists (established, agent-oriented, heavier machinery); plain rubric documents per artifact type (G-Eval criteria+steps form — simplest, but loses the scenario framing that binds a test to a concrete situation). RECOMMENDED SHAPE: keep Gherkin as the authoring surface (PO literacy), define the fitness-test artifact type with the falsifiability and segregation rules above, and specify a mechanical 1:1 compilation from Then-clauses to rubric assertions in an established judge format (promptfoo llm-rubric or equivalent) so the judged semantics rest on established tooling rather than a bespoke runner.

result.area_summary: Survey of established forms for writing down "what good looks like" for authored content. Five distinct form-families emerged, and they compose rather than compete. (1) DESCRIPTOR RUBRICS (educational assessment): a criteria-by-levels matrix where each cell is a prose description of observable performance — analytic (per-criterion judgment; best for feedback), holistic (one all-criteria judgment; best for quick triage), and single-point (describe only the proficient standard, annotate deviations) variants; the AAC&U VALUE rubrics are the mature exemplar, with a Definition + Framing Language + Glossary preamble ahead of the matrix and explicit instruction to localize the language. This family is the natural form for the requested SMALL qualitative fitness-test sets over non-deterministic LLM output, because it grades a continuum instead of forcing binary pass/fail. (2) BINARY QUALITY GATES: Scrum's Definition of Done (one uniform itemized quality contract applied to every increment; unmet = not releasable), per-item acceptance criteria (rule-oriented lists or scenario-oriented Given/When/Then), and Gawande-style checklists (pause points, DO-CONFIRM vs READ-DO, 5–9 killer items, validated via the Gawande/Boorman Checklist-for-Checklists). Gates suit mechanical checks; the checklist-design constraints directly govern how derived mechanical checks should be sized and worded. (3) QUALITY-CHARACTERISTIC TAXONOMIES: ISO/IEC 25010's characteristic→sub-characteristic hierarchy supplies shared vocabulary but no thresholds — a naming layer under which concrete criteria hang. (4) STYLE-GUIDE GOVERNANCE: Google's and Microsoft's writing style guides share a form — condensed highlights/top-10, voice principles, topical rule pages, an A–Z word list, and an explicit precedence hierarchy (project sheet → this guide → third-party references) — and the Vale linter demonstrates the exact pattern the shopsystem principle demands: mechanical checks DERIVED from the prose guideline, packaged per-guide, with severity tiers and per-project overrides. (5) OPERATIONALIZATION DISCIPLINE: Deming's operational definition (test procedure + criterion + yes/no decision) is the root discipline all the others instantiate — any quality adjective in a definition that lacks these three elements is not yet checkable. Two cross-cutting structural devices recur and are worth adopting wholesale: the normative/informative split (WCAG's testable success criteria vs its non-binding Techniques; VALUE's framing language vs its matrix) which maps cleanly onto "definition compiled into context" vs "derived checks"; and leveled conformance (WCAG A/AA/AAA, VALUE Benchmark→Capstone) for graded strictness. Code-review practice contributes a two-layer rubric form: one senior decision principle (Google: approve when the change definitely improves overall code health) plus an enumerated list of aspects to examine (design, functionality, complexity, tests, naming, comments, style, documentation), descending from Fagan's checklist-driven inspections. Recommended seed-layer composition: Deming discipline as the meta-rule for all definitions; analytic/single-point rubrics for qualitative fitness tests; DoD + Gawande constraints for mechanical gates; Gherkin for per-behavior acceptance (already in house); style-guide-plus-Vale as the enforcement architecture; ISO 25010 taxonomy form (not necessarily its content) for organizing characteristics.

findings.name: Analytic vs holistic rubric design (educational assessment)
findings.citation: Susan M. Brookhart, How to Create and Use Rubrics for Formative Assessment and Grading (ASCD, 2013), ISBN 9781416615071
findings.what_it_defines: The canonical rubric form: a set of criteria (about the quality being demonstrated, not the task) crossed with performance-level descriptions along a continuum of quality. Distinguishes analytic rubrics (each criterion judged separately) from holistic rubrics (all criteria applied at once for a single judgment), and general rubrics (reusable across tasks) from task-specific ones.
form_elements: Criteria naming qualities of the work, not steps of the task
Ordered performance levels (typically 3–5)
Prose performance-level descriptors per cell describing observable features, not evaluative adjectives
Analytic variant: one judgment per criterion (diagnostic, feedback-oriented)
Holistic variant: one overall judgment using all criteria simultaneously (fast, summative)
General vs task-specific scoping decision
findings.fit_notes: Directly applicable as the form for qualitative fitness tests on LLM output: an analytic rubric per artifact type gives per-criterion verdicts an LLM judge or human reviewer can defend; Brookhart's rule that descriptors must describe observable features rather than repeat evaluative adjectives ('good', 'clear') is the same demand Deming's operational definition makes, and is the key discipline when compiling definitions into a generating agent's context. Holistic form fits cheap triage passes; analytic form fits review rubrics derived from construction definitions.

findings.name: AAC&U VALUE rubrics
findings.citation: Association of American Colleges & Universities, VALUE (Valid Assessment of Learning in Undergraduate Education) rubrics, 16 rubrics developed 2007–2009 by national faculty teams; e.g., Critical Thinking VALUE Rubric
findings.what_it_defines: Sixteen analytic rubrics for hard-to-measure qualities (critical thinking, written communication, inquiry and analysis...). Each rubric is a one-page matrix of criteria rows against four named performance levels — Capstone (4), Milestone (3), Milestone (2), Benchmark (1) — preceded by a Definition of the outcome, Framing Language explaining scope and intended use, and a Glossary of terms used in the descriptors. Explicitly intended for institution-level assessment of authentic work, not grading, and explicitly meant to be translated into local language.
form_elements: Definition section stating what the quality is
Framing Language section bounding applicability and use
Glossary pinning descriptor vocabulary
Criteria rows (typically 4–6)
Four named, ordered levels: Capstone / Milestone / Milestone / Benchmark
Cell descriptors written as progressively more sophisticated observable behaviors
Explicit localization instruction: translate core expectations into local vocabulary
findings.fit_notes: The strongest existing exemplar of a governed rubric ARTIFACT (not just rubric theory): the Definition + Framing Language + Glossary preamble is exactly the 'construction definition' the seed layer wants to compile into agent context, with the matrix as the derived review rubric. The Benchmark→Capstone ladder is a ready-made graded-strictness scheme for LLM document quality (e.g., draft-acceptable vs publishable). Content is education-specific; adopt the form, not the rubrics.

findings.name: Single-point rubric
findings.citation: Jarene Fluckiger, "Single Point Rubric: A Tool for Responsible Student Self-Assessment," Delta Kappa Gamma Bulletin 76(4), 2010; University of Nebraska Omaha DigitalCommons
findings.what_it_defines: A rubric variant that describes ONLY the proficient standard for each criterion in a center column, with flanking blank columns for noting where the work falls short of or exceeds the standard. Eliminates the need to pre-author descriptors for every quality level.
form_elements: Criteria rows as in an analytic rubric
Single authored column: the proficient-standard descriptor per criterion
Blank 'concerns / not yet' column filled in per-assessment
Blank 'exceeds / advanced evidence' column filled in per-assessment
findings.fit_notes: Excellent fit for the 'definitions precede checks' principle at minimum authoring cost: the center column IS the construction definition, verbatim reusable in both the generating agent's context and the reviewer's rubric; deviations are recorded as free-text evidence rather than matched to pre-written level descriptors, which suits non-deterministic LLM output where failure modes are hard to enumerate in advance. Weaker for scoring/trending than full analytic rubrics because levels are not standardized.

findings.name: Definition of Done (Scrum)
findings.citation: Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, The 2020 Scrum Guide, section 'Increment / Definition of Done'
findings.what_it_defines: A quality contract: 'a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product.' One uniform, itemized list applied identically to every increment; an item not meeting it cannot be released or even shown at Sprint Review and returns to the backlog. Organizational DoD is a mandatory minimum that teams may extend; developers are accountable for conformance. Its stated function is transparency — shared understanding of what 'complete' means.
form_elements: Short itemized list of quality measures (verifiable states, not activities)
Uniform application to every unit of work — not per-item criteria
Binary consequence rule: unmet → not releasable, returns to backlog
Layering: organizational minimum + team/product extension
Named owner of conformance (Developers) and explicit transparency purpose
findings.fit_notes: The established form for the seed layer's cross-activity completion contract: every shopsystem activity definition's 'expected outcomes/outputs' section can take DoD form — a small list of verifiable end-states with an explicit consequence rule (the 'resulting action', including loop termination: work is done when DoD is met, else it re-enters the loop). Its uniform-gate character complements, and must not be confused with, per-item acceptance criteria. Directly adoptable; items must still pass Deming's operationalization test.

findings.name: Acceptance criteria: scenario-oriented (Gherkin) and rule-oriented formats
findings.citation: Gojko Adzic, Specification by Example (Manning, 2011); Gherkin language, Cucumber project reference documentation; rule-oriented vs scenario-oriented distinction as described in industry practice literature (e.g., AltexSoft's acceptance-criteria guide)
findings.what_it_defines: Per-work-item conditions of satisfaction, in two established formats: scenario-oriented — concrete examples in Given (context) / When (action) / Then (observable outcome) structure, one behavior per scenario, executable as tests; and rule-oriented — a bullet list of rules/constraints the result must satisfy, used when behavior examples are a poor fit (validations, cross-cutting rules, NFRs). Adzic's Specification by Example frames the underlying method: illustrate requirements with key examples and refine them into a living, executable specification.
form_elements: Given/When/Then scenario structure with one When/Then behavior per scenario
Concrete key examples rather than abstract statements
Rule-oriented variant: enumerated testable rules per item
Refinement loop: examples negotiated before construction, then automated
Living documentation: the criteria set remains the authoritative spec after delivery
findings.fit_notes: Already the shopsystem's canonical form (PO-authored Gherkin in features/), which validates the choice: scenario-oriented criteria are the per-item complement to a uniform DoD. For LLM-generated documents (as opposed to code), the rule-oriented variant plus key examples transfers better than executable Gherkin; Adzic's 'illustrate with key examples' maps directly onto small qualitative fitness-test sets — a handful of worked exemplar inputs/outputs pinned next to the definition.

findings.name: Google developer documentation style guide (governance form)
findings.citation: Google developer documentation style guide, publicly released September 2017 (Google Open Source Blog announcement), maintained at developers.google.com/style
findings.what_it_defines: The structural form of a governed prose style guide: an 'About' page declaring the guide's authority model, a Highlights page condensing the most important rules, topic pages of specific rules with correct/incorrect examples, a word list for term-level decisions, and — critically — an explicit reference hierarchy: project-specific style sheet overrides this guide, which overrides named third-party references (dictionary, external style manuals). Explicitly framed as guidelines to follow with judgment ('break the rules' clause), not law.
form_elements: Authority/precedence hierarchy: project sheet → this guide → named fallback references
Highlights page: condensed top rules for fast loading
Topical rule pages with before/after examples
A–Z word list for term-level rulings
Explicit non-normative stance with a break-the-rules escape clause
Continuous web publication rather than versioned print editions
findings.fit_notes: The precedence-hierarchy element is the most valuable import: the seed layer needs exactly this to resolve conflicts between shop-wide principles, artifact-type schemas, and per-BC conventions without duplicating rules. The Highlights form matches the context-compilation constraint — a condensed layer for the generating agent's prompt, with full topic pages as the reviewable definition of record. Adopt the form; the content is Google-product-specific.

findings.name: Microsoft Writing Style Guide (governance form)
findings.citation: Microsoft Writing Style Guide (2018–present, successor to the print Microsoft Manual of Style, 4th ed. 2012), Microsoft Learn
findings.what_it_defines: Same genre as Google's guide with two distinctive form elements: a small set of named brand-voice principles ('warm and relaxed, crisp and clear, ready to lend a hand') that sit above all specific rules, and a 'Top 10 tips for Microsoft style and voice' page as the compressed on-ramp; plus a 300+ term A–Z word list. Its governance story — retiring a versioned print manual in favor of a continuously updated web guide — is the modern maintenance model.
form_elements: Named voice principles as the top of the rule hierarchy
Top-10 tips page as compressed entry point
Bite-sized topical guidance pages
Large A–Z usage/terminology dictionary
Continuous online revision replacing print editions
findings.fit_notes: The voice-principles layer is the transferable idea: a handful of named, memorable principles that every specific rule must trace to — a good form for the seed layer's principle statements, keeping principle→rule derivation explicit. Verifies that two independent industry traditions converged on the same guide anatomy (principles, compressed highlights, topical rules, word list), which strengthens the case for adopting that anatomy rather than inventing one.

findings.name: Vale prose linter (derived-check enforcement model)
findings.citation: Vale, open-source syntax-aware prose linter (vale.sh); packages implementing the Microsoft and Google style guides as machine-checkable rules; see also LWN, 'Vale: enforcing style guidelines for text' (2024)
findings.what_it_defines: The enforcement architecture for prose guidelines: human-authored style guides are translated into YAML rule packages (regex/token/NLP checks), each rule carrying a severity (suggestion/warning/error) and a link back to the guideline it enforces; packages are versioned, synced per-project, and rules can be locally overridden or extended. Existing packages mechanize substantial portions of the Microsoft and Google guides.
form_elements: Rule = check pattern + severity tier + message + citation link to the source guideline
Style packages: a named, versioned bundle per style guide
Per-project configuration composing packages with local overrides
CI/editor integration so checks run at authoring time and gate time
Acknowledged residue: judgment rules stay prose-only; only operationalizable rules become checks
findings.fit_notes: This is the shopsystem's 'mechanical checks DERIVED from definitions' principle already running in the wild: definition (style guide) is authored first, checks are compiled from it, and each check cites its defining rule — the traceability the quality layer requires. The severity-tier and package/override model is worth copying for derived checks over LLM-generated documents; Vale itself is directly usable for the prose artifacts. Its honest split between mechanizable and judgment-only rules mirrors the mechanical-check vs review-rubric split in the task.

findings.name: ISO/IEC 25010 product quality model (SQuaRE)
findings.citation: ISO/IEC 25010:2023, Systems and software engineering — Systems and software Quality Requirements and Evaluation (SQuaRE) — Product quality model (revising ISO/IEC 25010:2011)
findings.what_it_defines: A hierarchical quality-characteristic taxonomy: nine top-level characteristics in the 2023 revision (functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, interaction capability, reliability, security, maintainability, flexibility, safety), each decomposed into named, defined sub-characteristics. Deliberately a reference vocabulary, not a threshold set: companion SQuaRE standards (25002 quality models, 2502n measures, 25030 quality requirements) turn characteristics into concrete measures and requirements.
form_elements: Two-level taxonomy: characteristic → sub-characteristic, each with a one-sentence definition
Separation of model (vocabulary) from measures and from requirements (thresholds) across companion standards
Claimed-completeness reference model used to check quality requirements for coverage gaps
Versioned revision process (2011 → 2023) with characteristics added/renamed
findings.fit_notes: Adopt the FORM — a small named taxonomy with per-node definitions, used as a coverage checklist when writing any artifact-type's quality criteria ('which characteristics does this definition address, which are consciously out of scope?'). The model/measure/requirement separation is a clean pattern for keeping construction definitions distinct from derived checks. The content is software-product-oriented and the standard is paywalled; for LLM-generated code the characteristic names supply shared review vocabulary, but a document-quality taxonomy would need its own nodes.

findings.name: Operational definitions (Deming)
findings.citation: W. Edwards Deming, Out of the Crisis (MIT Press, 1986), ch. 9, 'Operational Definitions, Conformance, Performance'
findings.what_it_defines: The requirement that any quality adjective be given 'communicable meaning' before it can be used in specification or judgment: 'Adjectives like good, reliable, uniform, round, tired, safe, unsafe, unemployed have no communicable meaning until they are expressed in operational terms of sampling, test and criterion.' An operational definition consists of three required elements: (1) a specific test procedure applied to the material or assembly, (2) a criterion for judgment, (3) a decision rule yielding yes or no — the item did or did not meet the criterion.
form_elements: Named concept being operationalized
Specified test/sampling procedure (who measures, how, on what)
Explicit criterion the measurement is compared against
Binary decision rule
Acknowledgment that the definition is a convention agreed for a purpose, revisable, not a claim of true meaning
findings.fit_notes: The root discipline of the entire seed layer: it is the acceptance test for every definition the layer produces. Any construction definition, DoD item, rubric descriptor, or guideline rule containing an unoperationalized adjective ('clear', 'concise', 'well-structured') is by Deming's standard not yet a check — for LLM-judged qualitative criteria, the 'test' element becomes the judge procedure plus the descriptor it compares against, which is exactly why rubric descriptors must be observable-feature language. Recommend adopting the three-element test as a meta-rule applied to all other seed-layer forms.

findings.name: Checklist design principles (Gawande/Boorman)
findings.citation: Atul Gawande, The Checklist Manifesto: How to Get Things Right (Metropolitan Books, 2009); Gawande, Boorman (Boeing) et al., 'A Checklist for Checklists,' Project Check
findings.what_it_defines: Design constraints that make checklists effective rather than harmful: choose between DO-CONFIRM (perform from memory, then pause and confirm) and READ-DO (read each item, then do it); anchor each checklist to a defined pause point in the workflow; restrict to roughly 5–9 'killer items' — steps dangerous to skip yet commonly missed — not comprehensive task inventories; keep usage under ~60–90 seconds; use precise wording in the language of the practitioners; and validate in real use before trusting. The companion 'Checklist for Checklists' is itself a meta-rubric with Development, Drafting, and Validation sections.
form_elements: Type declaration: DO-CONFIRM vs READ-DO
Named pause point triggering the checklist
5–9 killer items per pause point; omit what is never missed
Brevity budget (~60–90 seconds)
Exact, practitioner-language wording per item
Field-test-and-revise validation loop
Meta-checklist (Development/Drafting/Validation) governing checklist creation
findings.fit_notes: Directly governs the seed layer's mechanical gates: an LLM agent's derived checks should be typed (READ-DO for procedures the agent executes; DO-CONFIRM for post-generation verification passes), anchored to explicit pause points (activity termination, pre-dispatch, pre-commit) — which also supplies the requested form for 'resulting actions including termination' in process definitions. The killer-item constraint is the antidote to the LLM-native failure mode of bloated exhaustive checklists that dilute attention. The Checklist-for-Checklists is adoptable nearly verbatim as the quality gate for the quality layer's own checklist artifacts.

findings.name: Software inspection checklists (Fagan tradition)
findings.citation: Michael E. Fagan, 'Design and code inspections to reduce errors in program development,' IBM Systems Journal 15(3), 1976, pp. 182–211; Brian Brykczynski, 'A survey of software inspection checklists,' ACM SIGSOFT Software Engineering Notes 24(1), 1999
findings.what_it_defines: The original checklist-driven review form: inspections as a staged process with defined participant roles, entry/exit criteria per stage, and defect-type checklists derived from historical defect data to direct reviewer attention; defects classified and counted (per KLOC) to feed process improvement. Fagan reported inspections finding 38 defects/KLOC vs 8 for unit test on the studied system. Brykczynski's survey catalogs the subsequent 20+ years of published inspection checklists and their construction.
